19805-the-tale-of-mr-tod:
Beatrix Potter published The Tale of Mr. Tod in 1912. Mr. Tod is a fox, and Tommy Brock is a badger. Brock only occasionally eats rabbit pie, the tale confides. He takes very little young ones when other food is really scarce. Brock and old Mr. Bouncer share a dislike of the wicked otters and Mr. Tod. They often talk over that painful subject together.

Mr. Tod is among Potter's darkest tales. Benjamin Bunny's children are stolen for a fox's supper. Tommy Brock, no hero himself, becomes the rescue. Potter wrote it for older children and kept the danger real. Her watercolors and prose stay exact and unsentimental. It is a summit of her art.
20157-the-call-of-the-blood:
Robert Hichens published The Call of the Blood in 1905, a novel of love and fate. A woman takes letters from her writing-table drawer with care. She awaits a visit from their writer, Emile Artois, that day. He has wired that he comes from Paris by night train and boat.

Hichens sets much of the tale in Sicily, under a hot southern sun. The call of the blood means deep pulls of race, place, and passion. His characters feel forces they can barely name or resist. Readers get lush, tense romance in the style that made Hichens famous.
20219-the-lion-s-brood:
Duffield Osborne published The Lion's Brood in 1901, a novel of ancient Rome. A man wakes to find a coin turned in his hand as he dozed. Its reverse shows a horseman in full armor at the gallop. The rider brandishes a naked sword and grips a severed head by its hair.

That grim coin sets the tone for a tale of Rome's hard men. Osborne wrote of eagles, legions, and the brood that Rome bred for war. Battles and honor codes drive his Romans far more than ease. Readers get a vivid, blood-stained romance of the ancient world.
20846-handwork-in-wood:
Thanks to tool firms in New Haven, Chicago, and Beloit open William Noyes's Handwork in Wood. Their loan of electrotypes helped the book's many plates take shape. Stanley Rule and Level of New Britain stands among those thanked by name.

Noyes, a teacher at Teachers College, wrote a full guide to wood craft. Timber, tools, joints, and design unfold in set order with clear plates. The book served school shops that taught hand skill as mind training. Its mix of craft lore and teaching method still speaks to woodworkers who learn best by doing, step by careful step.
21074-afloat-on-the-flood:
Lawrence J. Leslie set this boys' novel in the town of Carson, where spring rain has sent the Evergreen River on the rampage. Published in Chicago in 1915, it follows young Max and his friends as floodwater rises around their homes. Chapters move from weather reports at the post office to rescues on a shaking bridge.

The boys lend a helping hand, shelter in a half-drowned farmhouse, and take refuge on a roof. Later they defend their camp against a wild dog pack and face unwelcome guests. The flood itself is the main villain, and the story ends as the waters fall.
21697-the-red-man-s-revenge-a-tale-of-th:
R. M. Ballantyne sets The Red Man's Revenge on the Red River, in a tale tied to a great flood. Ballantyne served as a clerk of the Hudson's Bay Company at the Red River Settlement from 1841. He worked there until 1847 and came home to Edinburgh in 1848.

His letters home, full of backwoods life, pushed his family to urge a book. The Young Fur Traders, Ungava, and The Coral Island grew from that start. In his last years his pen slowed, though his quality never failed. This tale returns to the ground he knew best, the northern Canadian settlement of his youth.
22012-the-rover-boys-on-a-hunt-or-the-my:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote The Rover Boys on a Hunt for the long Rover Boys series. It appeared in 1920. Jack Rover and his cousins are finishing the term at Putnam Hall when the story opens with a bobsled race. Christmas at home and a railroad rescue follow before the boys head north to Cedar Lodge.

Winter camp gives them hunting, ice fishing, and unwelcome visitors. Wolves prowl the woods, and a strange house deep in the trees raises questions no one can answer at first. The boys meet each scrape with jokes and teamwork. It is a brisk sample of the series fiction American boys devoured a century ago.
23223-good-blood: Ernst von Wildenbruch's Good Blood opens in a pleasant town known for its retired gentlemen. One of them, an old retired colonel, is known to everyone in town. He belongs to a colony of the superannuated, men who have settled down in this agreeable place to drag out the end of their days, wearily, in retirement.
annals-of-a-quiet-neighbourhood:
Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood, by George MacDonald, records a country vicar's first years among his parishioners at Marshmallows. MacDonald gives the narrator thirty four chapters of small events: despondency and consolation, a first Sunday, a first Monday, and a coffin. Visitors come from the Hall, the bishop's basin causes talk, and the new man preaches on God and Mammon to a congregation still deciding what he is.

Later chapters follow the organist, a Christmas party, and the Weir family, whose troubles fill three headings about devils in father, daughter, and vicar alike. Dr Duncan tells his story, the church rate stirs a fight, and an invalid tests everyone's patience. MacDonald writes sermons into daily life rather than the other way round: doctrine is what happens when a pastor must bury, marry, forgive, and be forgiven in one small place.
boswell-s-life-of-johnson-abridged-and-e:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson appears here abridged and edited by Charles Grosvenor Osgood, professor of English at Princeton. Osgood's preface explains his cuts: most criticism, notes, legal opinions, and letters go, while the conversation and the passages readers find by opening at random stay. Enough remains, he hopes, to illustrate the whole book.

What survives is Johnson talking: on arts propagated by Roman conquest, on biography, poetry, and men, with Boswell prompting and recording. A visitor cutting bristles from Johnson's hearth-broom as a relic shows the Doctor's fame from inside. The abridgement made the greatest English biography portable for students, and its Johnson, diverted by his own fancy, loses little of his force.
boyhood:
Leo Tolstoy continued Nikolenka's story in Boyhood, the second part of his early trilogy, in C. J. Hogarth's translation. The family leaves the estate at Petrovskoe for Moscow after the mother's death, and Nikolenka travels with his brother Woloda, their sisters, and the faithful tutor Karl Ivanitch. A thunderstorm on the road opens the boy's inner weather.

In Moscow come a grandmother's grief, bad marks at school, stolen keys, first loves, and long arguments about life. Karl Ivanitch tells his own history across three chapters. Tolstoy watches an adolescent discover vanity, cruelty, and conscience in himself, often within one page. Boyhood has less plot than Childhood and more mind: it is a diary of becoming, kept with merciless honesty.
captain-blood: Captain Blood, Rafael Sabatini's famous pirate adventure. The doctor turned buccaneer sails the Caribbean. This book preserves that swashbuckling classic. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-blackwoo:
Adam Blackwood was an author born at Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1539, who died in 1613. A great-nephew of Orkney's Bishop Robert Reid, he was educated at Paris after both parents died. The bishop provided for his schooling, and Queen Mary's generosity let him finish his studies at Paris and Toulouse. At Paris he taught philosophy and published a funeral poem on Charles IX in 1574.

He also published a work on religion and government in 1575; Archbishop James Beaton then recommended him to Mary for the judgeship of the Parliament of Poitiers, where he married Catherine Courtinier. Blackwood built a good library and wrote several books, including an Apology for Kings denouncing Buchanan's views and a vigorous defence of Queen Mary, published at Paris after her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adulteration-:
Adulteration of food, from Latin adulterare, to pollute, is defined as adding any non-condimental substance to a food, where that substance forms no portion of the food. Even this careful definition is imperfect, since heavily salted provisions may need soaking to remove salt, yet that is not adulteration. Food adulteration has long been practised, mentioned for bread by Pliny, who also notes Rome's trouble procuring pure wines.

Athens kept a public inspector of wines, and England and France early passed laws against bread adulteration. As far back as Edward the Confessor, public punishment awaited brewers of bad ale; adulteration's legal status rests largely on statute and varies by government. Food counts as adulterated if a substance depreciates or harms it. It also counts if cheaper matter is substituted, if a valuable constituent is removed, if it is an imitation, or if colouring improves its looks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-of-th:
A Spanish Carmelite called A. de Olivera, Anthony of the Mother of God was born at Leon in Old-Castile and died in 1641. At the University of Alcalá de Henares, Complutum, he taught Aristotle's dialectics and natural philosophy. Together with colleagues, he set out to make an encyclopaedia for students in arts and philosophy.

That work, first styled Collegium Complutense philosophicum and printed at Alcalá in 1624, saw further editions at Frankfurt in 1629 and at Lyons in 1637, 1651, and 1668. Thomists held it in high esteem. At first it was a treatise on logic. Over time, metaphysics and moral philosophy joined it, and it served as an introduction to the Salmanticenses' great Course of Theology. Anthony is also credited with the first three volumes of that Course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
Confraternities devoted to the Precious Blood, the blood of Christ, first appeared in Spain. The life of Francis of the Infant Jesus, a Carmelite lay brother who died in 1601, mentions such a confraternity at Valencia. A few years on they must have been numerous, since Anna of St. Augustine, who died in 1624, welcomed collectors of alms for Precious Blood confraternities erected in many places. Ravenna in Italy had one very early, and Rome had one under Gregory XIII, later merged with the Gonfalone.

The archconfraternity as it now stands owes its origin to Mgr. Albertini, then serving at San Nicola in Carcere, Rome, where devotions to the Precious Blood had been held since 1708. Moved by the temporal and spiritual misery of the French Revolution, he joined on 8 December 1808 all willing to meditate frequently on the Precious Blood into a society. That society grew into an archconfraternity able to affiliate others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-association-o:
The Association of the Holy Childhood is a children's association for foreign missions, founded twenty years after the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, in 1843. It was founded by Charles de Forbin-Janson, bishop of Nancy in France, as the Society of the Holy Childhood. Its end is twofold. First, to gather little Christian children around the Infant Jesus from tender years. Growing in age and strength and imitating Jesus their master, they practise charity toward their own perfection.

Second, by charity and enduring liberality, those same children may help save from death and sin the many thousand children in pagan countries such as China. Those children are neglected by parents and cast away to die without baptism. The association seeks baptism for abandoned ones and, should they live, training as craftsmen, teachers, doctors, or other members of Christian communities. The entry presents child charity organized for child rescue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-she:
Blessed Thomas Sherwood, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in London in 1551, he died at Tyburn on 7 February 1578. His parents also suffered for conscience, both enduring prison for the faith. After school in 1566 he helped his father, a woollen draper, for ten years, then set out for Douai to study for the priesthood.

Spotted in Chancery Lane, he was betrayed by George Marten and examined on the pope's bull and twice racked to learn where he had heard Mass. Cast naked into a dark, foul dungeon on bare earth, with only straw from a friend's pleading, he kept a cheerful courage. Tried on 3 February for denying the queen's supremacy, he was executed four days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-hosp:
The Brothers Hospitallers of Saint John of God carry on their founder's hospital charity from Granada across the world. John, born at Montemor Novo in 1495, turned to God's service at forty, founded his first hospital at Granada, and served the sick with heroic charity until his death in 1550. Canonized in 1690, he became patron of the dying and of all hospitals in 1898.

Antoni Martin succeeded him, Philip II funded hospitals at Madrid, Cordova, and beyond, and Pius V approved the order under Augustine's rule in 1572. Gregory XIII gave them Rome's Hospital of Saint John Calybita in 1584 as mother-house, and Marie de' Medici founded their first French hospital at Paris in 1601. The Revolution expelled them from forty hospitals holding 4,125 patients, yet the order now counts eleven provinces, 102 hospitals, and 12,978 beds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles-Francois Gounod, born at Paris in 1818 and dead there in 1893, stands among the great French composers of the nineteenth century. His father died while Charles was still a child, leaving his education to his mother. At the Lycée Saint-Louis he ranked among the best scholars. His musical gifts were carefully developed by his mother.

At thirteen his mother took him to Rossini's Otello, and that same year Mozart's Don Juan raised him to high enthusiasm. Mozart remained his ideal throughout his career, and Beethoven's Pastoral and Ninth Symphonies also left lasting marks. After study at the Conservatoire under Reicha and Lesueur, he returned to Paris in 1842. His career then turned to the operatic stage, where his lyrical, sentimental treatment of Faust, Romeo and Juliet, and Polyeucte became the widest expression of French Romanticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-h:
An entry on Christopher Holywood, Jesuit, born at Artane near Dublin in 1559. His family took its name from Holywood village. Holywood studied at Padua, then joined the Society of Jesus in 1579 at Dôle, to teach Scripture and theology at Pont-à-Mousson, Ferrara, and Padua, where he knew Bellarmine. Sent to Ireland in 1598, he was seized on the way and held in the Gatehouse, the Tower, and Wisbech Castle.

Freed after Elizabeth's death, Holywood reached Ireland on Saint Patrick's Eve 1604 and published two Latin controversial works at Antwerp that year. As superior of his brethren, in an Ireland without bishops, he reconciled the lapsed, settled quarrels, and healed wounds left by persecution. Only four Jesuits stood in Ireland when he landed, but forty-two worked there at his death in 1626, with sixty more in training or teaching abroad. His letters light up the country's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Ulrich Müller's entry follows the Most Precious Blood congregation, secular priests in community whose principal aim is missions and retreats. Members take no vows, held by charity's bond and a promise not to leave without permission. Pius VII, returning from exile, distressed at Rome's state, desired missions throughout the Papal States. He chose Gaspare del Bufalo with zealous priests in 1814, assigning San Felice convent at Giano, founded 15 August 1815.

New houses opened, and in 1820 six missions rose in the Campagna for banditti. Leo XII's 1823 election checked growth, misinformation clouding the society's standing. America received it in 1844 at Cincinnati Bishop Purcell's request, with year-long probation before brothers take fidelity promises or students begin study. Statistics count Italy's three provinces and fifteen houses, Rome, Albano, San Paolo leading, plus Spain's one province. A separate Mantua knight-order of 1608, founded by Duke Vincenzo Gonzaga with Paul V's approval, closes it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
The entry surveys Precious Blood congregations, opening with the Bernadines, nuns no longer in existence, founded by Mother Ballou with Saint Francis de Sales from reformed Cistercianesses. Spiehermans founded the Daughters at Sittard, Holland, in 1862, approved by Leo XIII's decree of 12 July 1890. Girls' education and sick care form their main object. A red girdle and a cross marked F.P.S. on red ribbon distinguish them. Cardinal Mazzella served as protector, Koningbosch holds the mother-house, and they assist Holy Ghost Fathers in German East Africa, with no American foundation yet.

Sister Adorers, established on 14 September 1861, lead a further section. Sisters of the Precious Blood at Gurtweil in Baden and Grisons, Switzerland, date to 1833 under Maria Anna Brunner with her son. Statistics for 1911 count 592 professed sisters, 48 novices, 26 postulants, and 6,954 pupils across Cleveland, Fort Wayne, Kansas City, Nashville, Saint Joseph, and Tucson dioceses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-of-th: This 1913 reference piece on Dominic of the Mother of God — the Passionist of England. Arthur Devine honors his missionary toil. His preaching shook the Victorian towns. The order prized its English pioneer. The apostle of the English missions. His Aston Hall mission is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ephod: This 1913 reference article on the ephod — the high priest's vestment. Anthony Maas unfolds its curious form. The gold and blue adorned the breast. The Urim shone in the sacred pouch. The robe of the Aaronic priesthood. Its Exodus form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etymology-of-: A 1913 entry on the etymology of the word God — the name's roots. Patrick Toner unfolds the scholars' theories. The Teutonic tongues yield the old word. The philologists sift the kindred forms. The origin of the sacred name. Its guth theory is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-existence-of-: A 1913 entry on the existence of God — the proofs of the reason. Patrick Toner unfolds the classic five. The motion proves the Prime Mover. The design bespeaks the wise Artificer. The demonstrations of the natural theology. Its quinque viae are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-: A 1913 entry on the Most Precious Blood's feast — the July devotion. Ulrich Müller unfolds its Roman origin. Pius hallowed the saving stream. The Church honors the redeeming Blood. The feast of the crimson price. Its July first is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friends-of-go: This 1913 reference article on the Friends of God — the Rhenish mystics. Reginald Walsh unfolds their quiet fellowship. Tauler was the famous preacher. The merchants sought the hidden life. The Gottesfreunde of the fourteenth century. Their 14th-century circle is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspard-mermi: This 1913 reference article on Mermillod — the Bishop of Lausanne. Patricius Schlager honors his exiled zeal. He shepherded the Swiss flock. The sacred college knew its fearless son. The confessor of the Kulturkampf. His 1892 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-god: This 1913 reference piece on God — the Supreme Being. The entry unfolds the classic proofs. Reason climbs to the First Cause. Faith crowns the natural light. The treatise of the divine nature. Its existence proofs are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good: This 1913 reference piece on the good — the being's perfection. James Fox unfolds its classic kinds. The will seeks the known end. The schools weigh the subtle term. The object of the moral appetite. Its transcendentals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hakon-the-goo: This 1913 reference article on Hakon the Good — Norway's Christian king. Pius Wittman unfolds his fateful reign. He planted the northern faith. The sagas bless the gentle name. The apostle of the Norwegian realm. His 961 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herod: This 1913 reference piece on Herod — the Idumean king. John Tierney unfolds his blood-stained reign. He slew the Bethlehem babes. The age knew the cruel lord. The tyrant of the Nativity's tale. His 4 BC death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-synod: A 1913 entry on the Holy Synod — Russia's church board. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its Petrine tale. Peter curbed the patriarch's throne. The tsars ruled the humbled Church. The consistory of the Russian Church. Its 1721 founding is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hood: This 1913 reference piece on the hood — the cowl's covering. Joseph Braun unfolds its vesture's use. The monks veiled the shaven crown. The choir keeps the seemly cloth. The capuce of the religious habit. Its amice is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jasper-and-jo: This 1913 reference piece on the Heywoods — the Jesuit brothers. Kate Mary Warren honors their English labors. Their pens served the persecuted faith. The order prized its gifted sons. The sixteenth century knew their names. Their 1598 deaths are famed. Their 1598 labors are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kingdom-of-go: A 1913 entry on the Kingdom of God — the Gospel's reign. Hugh Pope unfolds its sacred lore. Christ proclaimed the coming rule. The Church keeps the ancient hope. The faithful await its fullness. Its parables are famed. Its 1907 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mazenod: A 1913 entry on Mazenod — the Marseilles bishop. Adrian Morice honors his Oblate sons. His zeal served the youthful poor. France bless the mighty name. The nineteenth century knew his sway. His 1861 death is famed. His 1816 Oblates are famed. His 1816 missionary Oblates are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nature-and-at: What is God like? This entry surveys His nature and attributes: unity, truth, goodness, omnipotence, eternity, understood by analogy. The summit of theology, systematically climbed: each attribute reveals another facet of the divine nature, from eternity to mercy to love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nemrod: Nimrod was the mighty hunter before the Lord who founded the first kingdoms at Babel and Nineveh. This entry examines the Genesis account, the traditions about him, and his legend. The Bible's first empire-builder: his kingdom began at Babel's tower.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-servants: The Poor Servants of the Mother of God are the English sisters who serve the poor and sick. This entry covers their foundation, their rule, and their convents. The servants of Mary's poor: their quiet convents dot the English towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precious-bloo: The Precious Blood is Christ's blood shed for man's redemption. This entry treats its devotion, its feasts, and its theology. The price of the world's ransom: its July feast honors the sacred drops of Calvary's holy cross each passing year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presence-of-g: The presence of God is the devout remembrance that He is always near. This entry explains its practice, its fruits, and its masters. The recollection of the loving Eye: its constant habit sanctifies the whole working day in loving recollection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priesthood: The priesthood is the sacrament that configures men to Christ the Priest. This long entry examines its nature, its degrees, and its grace. The sacred character of orders: its indelible mark endures forever in heaven and on earth alike in Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rood: The rood is the great cross of the chancel screen. This entry explains its form, its history, and its devotion. The crucifix above the choir: its carved beam spans the screen in stone and wood and paint and gold and light.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-son-of-god: The Son of God is the second Person of the Trinity. This long entry examines His name, His divinity, and His incarnation. The Only-Begotten of the Father: His eternal Godhead fills the creeds of the Church in the councils of Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-disibod: St. Disibod was the hermit of the Nahe valley. This entry traces his cell, his Hildegard, and his cult. The Irishman of the Rhenish hills: his lonely cell crowned Disibodenberg in the 600s' Nahe in the hills of the Rhineland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-of-go: St. John of God was the founder of the Hospitallers. This long entry examines his Granada, his hospitals, and his fame. The patron of the sick nurses: his new hospitals filled Granada in the 1540s' Albaicín in the quarter of the Moors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synod: The synod is the council of the church. This long entry examines its kinds, its law, and its history. The assembly of the bishops: its solemn canons crowned the dioceses in the 300s of the Church in the empire of the Caesars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bridge-bu: The Bridge-Building Brotherhood were the pontiff friars. This entry traces their bridges, their charity, and their history. The brothers of the river crossings: their stone bridges crowned the Rhône in the 1170s of the pilgrims in the very old road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-highest-g: The Highest Good is the end of morals. This long entry examines its Aristotle, its Kant, and its schools. The supreme object of the will: its lofty idea crowned the schools in the 300s BC of the Lyceum in the grove.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-wood: Wood was the martyr of the west. This entry traces his 1500s, his seminary, and his death. The priest of the English mission: his brave death crowned the west in the 1580s of the mission in the very old hills.
childhood:
Leo Tolstoy made his name with Childhood, a short novel told by Nikolenka Irtenev, a boy of ten on a Russian country estate. Tolstoy was a young officer when the book first appeared, and C. J. Hogarth translated this edition. Nikolenka watches his German tutor Karl Ivanitch, his gentle mother, and his older brother Woloda with painful honesty.

Scenes move from lessons and birthday presents to hunts, dances, and a death that ends the boy's safe world. Nikolenka swings between love and shame, catching his own feelings in the act. Readers meet Tolstoy's gift early here: small moments, exact feelings, and a child's view that spares nobody, least of all himself.
clara-hopgood:
Clara Hopgood, by Mark Rutherford, studies conscience in a fen country town. Rutherford was the pen name of William Hale White. T Fisher Unwin printed this third impression in 1907. The first edition appeared in March 1896. Its title page names an editor, Reuben Shapcott, his other invented self. The story opens at Fenmarket, in the Fens, ten miles from Eastthorpe.

White notes that all roads out of Fenmarket run level. They run monotonous too, unlike the hill country at Eastthorpe's edge. The flatness suits his subject. Clara and her sister Madge Hopgood grew up in a strict Nonconformist home. Dissenters outside the Church of England shaped that home. Courtship, religious doubt, and family duty now test both sisters. Everyone watches everyone else. White wrote about provincial dissenting life from inside it. Ordinary happiness, refused and accepted, does the testing.

eastman-indian-boyhood:
Charles Eastman, a Santee Sioux writer and doctor, published Indian Boyhood in 1902. Eastman, also called Ohiyesa, grew up in the traditional way before his father took him into white schooling. The memoir looks back at that first world with love.

He describes hunting lessons, games, storytelling around winter fires, and the teaching of his grandmother and uncle. His people were then living the last years of free life on the northern plains. The reservation era was closing in as he wrote. Indian Boyhood became a beloved classic, the first of his many books joining Native memory to American letters.
hofmannsthal-der-tor-und-der-tod:
A shallow aesthete who has admired life instead of living it meets Death face to face in Hofmannsthal's Der Tor und der Tod, given here in German. Death and the Fool, written when the poet was nineteen, stages that reckoning in a single night. Claudio's beautiful rooms and collected treasures suddenly testify against him.

Figures from his past return to show him the loves and duties he let slip away unused. The verse play meditates on art, life, and mortality with stunning maturity. Its announcement of a genius was unmistakable to its first audiences. Short enough to read at a sitting, it leaves a long echo. The work still opens many editions of Hofmannsthal, rightly placed first.
love-songs-of-childhood:
Love-Songs of Childhood is a book of children's verses by Eugene Field. Field dated his dedication at Chicago on November 1, 1894. He lays the songs at the feet of the aunt who once rocked him to sleep. The contents list the Rock-a-By Lady, the Night Wind, and Kissing Time.

Verses here tell of gardens, cradles, storks, and the Dinkey-Bird. 'Jest 'Fore Christmas' and the Duel bring fun and mischief. Field mixes lullaby tenderness with sly humor for older readers. His 'Wynken, Blynken, and Nod' became America's best-known lullaby poem. The book made him the beloved children's poet of his age.
magnum-bonum-or-mother-carey-s-brood:
Magnum Bonum, or Mother Carey's Brood, is a family novel by Charlotte M. Yonge. The contents open with Joe Brownlow's fancy and a brood of 'chickens.' Mother Carey is a widow raising her children on small means. Her late husband left behind a secret he called his magnum bonum.

That 'great good' is an invention that might make a fortune. Chapters weigh brains against no brains, and flight against duty. An offer comes for the magnum bonum, testing the family's honor. Ellen's own magnum bonums prove to be of another kind. Yonge writes of home, sacrifice, and steady faith. It is among her warmest tales of family life.
marie-bashkirtseff-from-childhood-to-gir:
Marie Bashkirtseff: From Childhood to Girlhood draws on her famous journal. Mary J. Safford translated these pages from the French. Marie began her journal at twelve years old. She wrote, the editor says, ingenuously and sincerely, in notebooks bound in white parchment.

Her whims amuse, her enthusiasms thrill, and her sufferings touch the reader. The editor prized the book for revealing a young girl's true mind. Children, she notes, hide their real selves from grown-up people. Marie hid nothing: her irony and ambition fill every page. Very few documents show childhood from inside so clearly. These early notebooks open the soul of a remarkable girl.
my-boyhood:
John Burroughs recalls his youth on a New York farm in this memoir. His son Julian wrote the foreword and a closing part. Julian says his father wrote in self-defense against his own draft. The old farm sat high on the side of Old Clump.

Burroughs loved his birthplace and was homesick for it for years. Hills, chores, woods, and first books fill his sketches. A poem called Waiting opens the contents with calm faith. The memoir shows how a farm boy became America's famed nature writer. Its plain, fond voice makes the lost farm world live again on the page.
nasa-tm-19650014315-a-wind-tunnel-invest:
Langley researchers tested rounded nose shapes, called bodies of revolution, in a high Mach number jet at very high speeds. Angles of attack went all the way to ninety degrees, far beyond normal flight. The shapes began as a pointed nose, then were changed step by step in the tunnel program.

Blunting the nose, changing a hollow nose face to a rounded one, and adding afterbodies were all tried in turn. Results showed that planform area and its spread mattered more than the exact nose shape or sharpness. A cross-flow drag theory matched the measured normal-force data well in the comparison. Such high-angle data matter for missiles and for reentry shapes that must stay stable.
nasa-tm-19690000779-application-of-the-c:
John D. Warmbrod and Heinz G. Struck of Marshall Space Flight Center present a calculation method for tube wind tunnels in this August 1968 memorandum. The method computes one-dimensional, time-dependent compressible flow through a pressure-tube wind tunnel. Designers need such predictions before building and running a new tunnel.

The procedure uses the method of characteristics for unsteady flow of a perfect gas. It accounts for area changes, shock formation, and crossing discontinuities in the flow. A Fortran computer program for the CDC 3200 machine accompanies the method. Input preparation is described in detail. Calculated results are shown for a pressure-tube tunnel then under construction at Marshall.
nasa-tm-19720023239-nasa-dod-earth-orbit:
R. E. Kincade, M. E. Donahoo, and W. R. Pruett wrote this NASA internal note in July 1971. They worked in the Flight Analysis Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. Their subject was how a planned Earth orbit shuttle might carry payloads for NASA and the Defense Department.

The note builds traffic models based on loading payloads from end to end. It sets out spacecraft plans and space missions, and it counts flights and payload needs. It also weighs two possible reusable tugs for moving loads in orbit. Planners could use such models to judge how much traffic the shuttle system had to handle.
penrod: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Penrod, the dedication, contents, and the first sentence of chapter one, with no more story text visible. The title page names Booth Tarkington. The contents promise thirty-one chapters of a boy's scrapes, among them a boy and his dog, the pageant of the Table Round, the smallpox medicine, tar, and a birthday party. The opening line sets Penrod morosely on the back fence, envying Duke, his wistful dog.
queen-victoria-her-girlhood-and-womanhoo:
Queen Victoria: Her Girlhood and Womanhood, by Grace Greenwood, is a life of the Queen written for younger readers, opening with a letter that dedicates the book to Camilla Toulmin, Mrs. Newton Crosland, of Blackheath Park. The letter looks back to the days when the Victorian era itself was young.

In her preface Greenwood owns that the book was written in under three months. There were delays while she hunted facts about the Queen's early life. A serious trouble of her eyes delayed her too. Its style, she warns, is free and easy, formed by years of newspaper work, and new for the grave business of biography.
ranald-bannerman-s-boyhood: Ranald Bannerman's Boyhood, by George MacDonald, dated 1871, is shown here by its contents alone. The chapters run from an introductory and The Glimmer of Twilight through My Father, Kirsty, I Begin Life, and No Father, then school and trouble: Mrs. Mitchell Is Defeated, A New Schoolmistress, Sir Worm Wymble, two kelpie chapters, Wandering Willie, Elsie Duff, A New Companion, and I Go Down Hill, with the trouble still growing.
records-of-a-girlhood:
Frances Ann Kemble, the actress known as Fanny Kemble, recorded her early life in this memoir, issued in a second edition by Henry Holt of New York in 1880. Parts of it first ran in the Atlantic Monthly. A note at the front says much new matter was added and the whole was revised.

Kemble begins with a set of her own letters, written over forty years and sent back to her by a friend. The letters, in their thousands, form a history of her life as she lived it. Her girlhood in a famed stage family, and the start of her own career, lie ahead in that record.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
Montrose J. Moses edited this set of representative plays by American dramatists, dated 1856-1911 on its title page, and issued it in 1921. Each play carries his introduction, and portraits and original playbills picture the set. He dedicated the book to Brander Matthews, friend of the American theatre.

Ten plays fill the contents. Rip Van Winkle, in Charles Burke's version of 1850, leads, and Francesca da Rimini by George Henry Boker follows. Love in '76, Paul Kauvar, and Shenandoah carry the set through the century's turn. In Mizzoura, The Moth and the Flame, The New York Idea, The Easiest Way, and The Return of Peter Grimm close the list.
robin-hood:
J. Walker McSpadden retells the Robin Hood ballads in twenty chapters of prose, each headed with how the deed was done. The first tells how Robin Hood became an outlaw. Then come his meetings with Little John, Will Scarlett, and Friar Tuck, the three most famed of his merry men.

Robin turns butcher and enters the Sheriff's service in one chapter, and Little John enters it in the next. Allan-a-Dale's wooing is prospered, a widow's three sons are rescued, and Robin fights Guy of Gisbourne. Maid Marion comes back to Sherwood Forest, the outlaws shoot in King Harry's tourney, and the Bishop is dined and then goes outlaw-hunting. Will Stutely's rescue closes the list shown.
roman-mosaics-or-studies-in-rome-and-its:
Hugh Macmillan, D.D., gathered these studies of Rome and its neighbourhood in a book from Macmillan of London and New York in 1888. He had written Bible Teachings in Nature and Holidays in High Lands before it. Chapter one takes A Walk to Church in Rome, street by street.

The walk passes his residence in Capo le Case, the church of San Giuseppe, and the Pillar of the Immaculate Conception. The Piazza di Spagna, its staircase, models, and beggars follow, then the Via Babuino and the Piazza del Popolo. Chapter two turns to the Appian Way, its tombs, its loneliness, and its restoration, in the same close-watched manner.
rookwood:
William Harrison Ainsworth's novel Rookwood, dated 1834 in its heading, appears here from the Rittenhouse Press of Philadelphia. Thackeray's phrase, the immortal Ainsworth, heads the title pages, and the New York Herald is quoted for the book's vivid picture of its times and places. A frontispiece shows Dick Turpin clearing Hornsey toll-gate.

A table of contents supplied by the transcriber, not present in the original, maps the book. A memoir and a preface stand before Book One, The Wedding Ring. Its first parts are named The Vault and The Skeleton Hand, gothic titles for the tale that follows.
seekers-after-god:
Rev. F. W. Farrar, Canon of Westminster, wrote these lives of pagan thinkers who reached toward truths that Christians hold. The Seneca section opens the book. Farrar begins in Cordova, the Spanish city on the Guadalquivir that gave Rome the Seneca family.

Farrar shows how Spain shaped Roman letters, giving Rome emperors like Trajan and Hadrian and teachers like Quintilian. Seneca's father held knight's rank, and the son rose high at court. Farrar reads such lives with sympathy, honoring honest seeking after God in a world without the Christian faith he himself taught.
sentimental-tommy-the-story-of-his-boyho:
J. M. Barrie published this story of a boy's early years in 1896, after The Little Minister and A Window in Thrums had made his name. Tommy first appears at age five on a dirty London stair, in scant clothes that shame him. He will not beg, though hunger often tempts him.

His mother has warned him never to ask for food, and Tommy obeys with needless pride. Passing doors rich with the smell of fried fish, he calls out that he wants none of it. Barrie draws a proud, fanciful child whose lies and longings both spring from want, in prose both tender and sly.
sheila-of-big-wreck-cove-a-story-of-cape:
James A. Cooper wrote this Cape Cod tale, copyright as a book in 1922 after a serial run in 1921. A front picture by R. Emmett Owen shows a craft pointed out to Prudence. Contents open with Cap'n Ira and Prue, then the captain of the Seamew and a girl styled the Queen of Sheba.

Chapters follow a search for Ida May, a girl's own story, and a plot, before the scene settles at Big Wreck Cove. A new hand takes the helm there. Cooper mixes sea folk, young love, and hidden pasts in the salty, warm manner of his other Cape tales.
slavery-ordained-of-god:
Rev. Fred. A. Ross argues in Slavery Ordained of God that bondage forms part of the rule God set for fallen men in set states of life. The book is built from speeches he gave and letters he printed, not from stray pieces. Its text verse is Romans xiii. 1, on the powers that be. Ross speaks to men North and South who honor God's word.

His preface states one great idea, first put in a speech to the Presbyterian General Assembly at Buffalo on May 27, 1853. The North must learn, he says, that the master and slave tie is not sin in itself. The South must grant that bondage is an evil in some states of life, and that free and equal life ranks higher when its time comes.
spiritual-life-and-the-word-of-god: Emanuel Swedenborg, who lived from 1688 to 1772, wrote Spiritual Life and the Word of God, drawn from the Apocalypse Explained. The contents sort the work in four parts. The first treats how spiritual life is gained, the goods of charity, the shunning of evils, and the cleansing of the inside. The second walks through the commandments one by one, and the third treats the spoiling of good and truth in its kinds; the fourth treats the Divine Word and its senses.
stories-of-childhood:
Stories of Childhood forms one of the Little Classics volumes edited by Rossiter Johnson, printed by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1914, with an 1875 copyright behind it. The set gathers short pieces about children by well-known hands.

The contents open with Ouida's A Dog of Flanders, where the boy Nello and the great dog Patrasche are left alone in the world, friends closer than brothers. John Ruskin's King of the Golden River follows. Then come pieces by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps and John Brown. Henry Kingsley and Rebecca Harding Davis add tales. Charles Dickens closes with A Child's Dream of a Star.
the-blossoming-rod:
Mary Stewart Cutting wrote a family story published in New York by A. L. Burt and Doubleday, Page. Mr Langshaw senses unusual preparations for his Christmas gift, as children ask him for change to pay for services. Money limits, the narrator says, run through the family's dearest hopes.

On the Friday before Christmas, Langshaw stops at a sporting-goods shop and finds a ten-dollar bill in his pocket, a debt repaid that day. A trout-rod in the window, cut from fifteen dollars to ten, tempts him at last. He worries over his son George, aged ten, who shirks duty to his mother. Longing, thrift, and fatherhood meet at Christmas.
the-elephant-god:
Gordon Gasserly's The Elephant God, printed at New York in 1921, is set in the Terai forest of India. Its contents open with a secret mission and a rogue elephant, then a girl of the Terai and the madness of Badshah. Later chapters name a rajah's palace, a Bhutia raid, the rescue of Noreen, and the making of a god.

Gasserly sets the book, with wry thanks, to a rogue elephant that slew men and women and taught him much. Love, fever rites for Kali, and jungle peril drive this Raj tale of soldiers and planters.
the-existence-of-god:
The Existence of God opens with a frank bar: proofs from metaphysics lie past most men's reach. Its author, unnamed in these pages, says he cannot open his eyes without seeing the art that shines through all nature; the least glance shows him the hand that made all. Thinkers may trace first principles, he owns, and that road is sure, but its very simplicity hides it from most.

Few can work in pure thought; most lean on sense and image. So the book turns to the path of nature's works. Plain words and short sections carry a case once famed across Europe.
the-flood:
Emile Zola wrote The Flood as a short tale told by an old farmer of Saint-Jory, a village on the Garonne near Toulouse. Louis Roubien, aged seventy, tells how his house was blessed.

Roubien counts his kin at table: his brother Pierre, his sister Agathe, his son Jacques and wife Rosie, three granddaughters, and babes down to ten months. He was the richest farmer in the parish, with no bad crop in memory. Pride in that full house sets the height from which the river's rise will cast them. Zola builds dread from plain, warm facts.
the-good-news-of-god: Charles Kingsley wrote The Good News of God. It is a book of sermons. Macmillan and Co. printed it in London in 1887. It was first transferred from Longman and Co. in 1863. It was reprinted many times since. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of sermons. The heads name The Beatific Vision and The Glory of the Cross. They name The Life of God, Worship, and De Profundis. They name The Race of Life and True Repentance. No sermon text is present.
the-lances-of-lynwood:
Charlotte M. Yonge's preface to this tale of chivalry hopes for one effect. The sketch should tempt young readers to Froissart's chronicle. His tomes' size should not deter them. The Orthon tale is copied nearly word for word from Froissart. It resembles German and Irish legends of household spirits. The old French life of Bertrand du Guesclin supplied more material. Enrique of Trastamare arrives disguised as a palmer in it. She apologizes for aging Henry of Lancaster. She made him a year or two older than his birth warrants.

Chapter I opens in Edward III's reign. England's interior presented a peaceful, prosperous aspect then. Turbulent spirits were occupied in foreign wars. Wise government established plenty and security at home. A second record of this tale in this set prints the same matter. Its preface and opening chapter are identical in what is shown.
the-leatherwood-god:
William Dean Howells bases his novel on a real Ohio religious imposture drawn from Judge Taneyhill narrative in an Ohio Valley series. A publisher note says the main events and drama follow that account, while details and inner lives are invented. Some speeches of the imposter Dylks come from a witness report.

Illustration captions show Dylks towering over followers in a temple at Leatherwood, hair tossed like a mane. Howells studies how a poor settlement could accept a man claim of godhood. Faith, pride, and hardship make neighbors defend a fraud they helped create.
the-life-and-romances-of-mrs-eliza-haywo: George Frisbie Whicher wrote his Columbia University monograph on Eliza Haywood life and romances in 1915. Only the title page and contents are present here. Chapters cover her life and her short romances of passion. The Duncan Campbell pamphlets, secret histories, scandal novels, and her place as a heroine of The Dunciad follow in the list. A bibliography, a chronological list, and an index close the plan. The study itself cannot be seen in this record.
the-little-house-in-the-fairy-wood:
Ethel Cook Eliot wrote The Little House in the Fairy Wood, a children's fantasy in nineteen chapters. Their titles include Magic in a Mist, At the Heart of a Tree, and The Beautiful Wicked Witch. Chapter one introduces Eric, a boy woken roughly at six in the morning by Mrs. Freg, who shakes him and the two boys sharing his bed and orders them all up. That ordinary morning, the narrator promises, will begin everything new for Eric.

The contents point toward a bright house in a wood, a Tree Mother, a wind hunt, birthdays, and spring wandering. Young readers get a gentle magic story that starts in a hard, crowded household and opens into an enchanted forest world.
the-merry-adventures-of-robin-hood:
Howard Pyle addresses the reader directly in the preface to The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood. He warns serious plodders who feel shame at mirth to close the book at once. His pages, he says, show sober folk of real history frisking in gay colors and motley. A stout, quick-tempered fellow goes by the name of Henry II, and a fair lady is bowed to as Queen Eleanor.

Pyle also promises the Sheriff of Nottingham, the Bishop of Hereford in rich clerical robes, and Richard of the Lion's Heart feasting beside Robin. His setting is not Fairyland but the land of Fancy, built from old ballads snipped, clipped, and tied together again. In that country flowers bloom forever and ale flows like a brook. Readers, young ones especially, are invited through the curtain into No-man's-land, where Robin's company lives the merriest of merry lives.
the-mystery-of-edwin-drood:
Charles Dickens's The Mystery of Edwin Drood lists twenty-three chapters in its contents, from The Dawn to A Gritty State of Things Comes On and The Dawn Again. Chapter I, The Dawn, opens in a drugged confusion. A man stares at an ancient English cathedral tower. He cannot understand how it stands before him. No spike of rusty iron rises in the real prospect between his eye and the tower.

The spike belongs to a vision. Cymbals clash, and a Sultan passes in long procession to his palace. Ten thousand scimitars flash, and dancing girls strew the way. The imagined spike waits there for Turkish robbers to be impaled. Rochester Castle illustrates the chapter in this printing, grounding the vision in Dickens's cathedral town of Cloisterham.
the-poetical-works-of-thomas-hood:
The Poetical Works of Thomas Hood, in an enlarged and revised edition from A. L. Burt Company of New York, opens with a biographical introduction by William Michael Rossetti. There were scarcely any events in Hood's life, Rossetti begins. Two conditions ruled it: life-long ill health, and a commercial failure that drove him abroad for a time. Beyond those, the outward facts of an upright, beneficial career offer little for the record.

Hood's father kept a publishing and bookselling business in London's Poultry, as a partner in Vernor, Hood, and Sharpe. A Scotchman who came up early, he reprinted old works and published Bloomfield's poems, dealing handsomely with him. He also wrote two novels himself. Rossetti wishes more were known of those forgotten tales. The son's questions about the piteous woman of his Bridge of Sighs still interest readers.
the-subterranean-brotherhood:
Julian Hawthorne's prison book opens with a poem called Footfalls, written in Atlanta Penitentiary in May 1913. The poet listens at night to a step overhead. It paces the cell, four paces from barred door to iron wall and back. He answers the unknown brother above him. The hunger for lost life goads that pacing. He knows that hunger too.

A contents list then maps the memoir's route. An introductory chapter leads off. The devil's antechamber and the road to oblivion follow. Initiation and routine come next. Some prison friends of the author's close the heads. Poem and contents together announce a first-hand account of federal prison life, written from inside the subterranean brotherhood of the barred and caged, pent from earth, sky, and stars.
the-thin-red-line-and-blue-blood: Arthur Griffiths, author of The Chronicles of Newgate, published The Thin Red Line in two volumes with Chapman and Hall in 1886; this record covers volume one. Only its title page and opening contents are present. Nine chapters begin with a commissary called, an arrest and interrogation, a mousetrap, a spider's web, and war fever, then move onto dangerous ground with an old acquaintance and a southern pearl. The headings sketch a military crime story of the Crimean era, but Griffiths's chapters themselves stay outside this record.
the-truce-of-god:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Truce of God, published by George H. Doran in 1920 with decorations by Harold Sichel, opens on a grey, dreary Christmas Day that fell on a Saturday. The town at the hill's foot rejoices over a prosperous year, a fat steer dressed in the square amid heaps of fruit and vegetables. In his cliff-top castle the young overlord sulks and bites his nails. From Thursday evening to Monday morning the Church's Truce of God forbids his fighting.

For three full days each week his men-at-arms polish weapons and grow fat. Meanwhile his grudge against his cousin Philip, called the Black Beard, feeds on itself. The Bishop of Tours has come about scandalous reports: a lady has taken refuge with Philip. Rinehart, famous for mysteries, here writes a medieval tale of feud, sanctuary, and enforced peace.
unity-of-good: Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, wrote Unity of Good. It was first copyrighted in 1887. The pages here give the title page and contents only, so the essays themselves do not appear. The contents list short pieces, several framed as questions. Caution in the Truth asks whether God can behold sin, sickness, and death. Seedtime and Harvest asks whether anything the senses grasp is real. Other titles include The Deep Things of God, A Colloquy, The Ego, and Soul.
young-robin-hood:
G. Manville Fenn wrote this children's tale of young Robin Hood. It opens on a forest road with a small boy riding behind a sour serving man named David. The boy wriggles on the slippery horse and teases David about his size. David threatens to pitch him into the brambles. The boy laughs that his father would punish such an act.

David then tries fear instead, asking if the dark forest scares him. The boy denies any fear at all. That bold start fits a future outlaw hero. Readers get a lively, talk-filled opening. Fenn keeps the scene light while danger waits in the trees.
